title: Check yourself: counting, dumping and measuring concurrent code

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A connection pool keeps `idle` and `busy` in two `AtomicLong`s. `borrow()` runs `idle.decrementAndGet()` then `busy.incrementAndGet()`; `stats()` reads `idle`, then `busy`, and reports their sum. Two threads call `borrow()` once each while a third calls `stats()` once. What does trying every order of their steps show?

options.text: The pool has 90 orders and about half report a wrong sum, since another thread can run between the two calls in borrow()
options.says: borrow() and stats() are two calls each, so three threads have 6!/(2!2!2!) = 90 orders; in 46 of them stats() falls between a borrow's two writes

options.text: The pool has 90 orders and none reports a wrong sum, since idle and busy each change in one atomic call in borrow()
options.says: the sum spans two counters and nothing changes them at once, so a stats() between the two writes of a borrow() sees a wrong sum

options.text: The pool has 6 orders and none reports a wrong sum, since each AtomicLong call in borrow() is one step no thread can split
options.says: each call is atomic, but each method makes two calls and another thread can run between them, so there are 90 orders, not 3! = 6

options.text: The pool has 6 orders and about half report a wrong sum, since stats() can land between the two calls in borrow()
options.says: 6 orders is the count when each method is one step, as in a synchronized version, and then no order is broken; with two steps per method there are 90

origin.section: Each Step Other Threads Can Run Between Multiplies the Schedules: 6 for synchronized, 1,124 for Lock-Free

questions.stem: An inventory class updates two counters in two separate atomic calls. Its CI test starts two updates and one read together on a latch, 5,000 times per build, and has failed twice in a year. An exhaustive model of the same three calls finds the invariant broken in 40 % of the possible orders. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The broken orders need a third updater the test lacks, since most of the model's broken orders come from runs with three
options.says: the page's model breaks 520 of 1,124 schedules with only two holders and a check, and even 3 of 10 with one holder; a third thread only adds more

options.text: The broken orders need a gap that timing opens in few runs, since the two writes are only a few instructions apart
options.says: orders are not equally likely: the threads leave the latch at slightly different moments, so most runs execute one call after another

options.text: The broken orders do run in the test, but the read that would catch them comes after the two writes have both landed
options.says: a read between the two writes returns the wrong sum as soon as it runs, as the paused-writer run shows; the test fails rarely because it seldom produces that order

options.text: The broken orders do run in the test, but the CPU makes the second of the two writes visible together with the first
options.says: the paused-writer run shows the reader seeing the first write and not the second every time; the test fails rarely because it seldom produces that order

origin.section: A Stress Test Samples the Likely Schedules, So It Seldom Hits the Broken Ones

questions.stem: A payments service hangs. Its thread dump shows 12 threads `RUNNABLE` with `at FeeTable.acquire(FeeTable.java:31)` on top, each using a full core, and no `waiting to lock` line anywhere. Another thread, `RUNNABLE` with no CPU, is in a socket read called from `FeeTable.reload`. Which reading of this dump holds?

options.text: FeeTable's lock is a spin on an atomic flag, a kind of lock whose holder the JVM keeps no record of
options.says: only monitors and java.util.concurrent locks record an owner; a spin on an atomic shows RUNNABLE threads burning CPU with no owner and no '- locked' line

options.text: FeeTable's lock is a monitor, and a dump prints its `waiting to lock` lines only when taken with the -l option
options.says: threads waiting for a monitor print as BLOCKED with 'waiting to lock' and use no CPU, without any option; here the waiters are RUNNABLE and burn a core each

options.text: The reload thread let go of the lock when its read began, since a blocking socket read releases its thread's locks
options.says: a thread keeps every lock it holds while it blocks in I/O; the threads in acquire() are still waiting for it

options.text: The reload thread holds a ReentrantLock, and threads that wait for one stay RUNNABLE until the lock is released
options.says: a thread waiting for a ReentrantLock parks: it shows as WAITING, uses no CPU, and ThreadMXBean names the holder

origin.section: A Thread Dump Names a Monitor's Holder; a Hand-Rolled Lock Shows Only Busy Threads

questions.stem: A rate limiter keeps two counts behind `synchronized` and handles 3 million calls a second on 16 threads in a tight-loop benchmark. A colleague's rewrite keeps the counts in two `AtomicLong`s and handles 7 million. Production peaks at 40,000 calls a second. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep the synchronized version, since 3 million a second is about 75 times the 40,000 peak it has to carry
options.says: the simple design's cost under contention is real but irrelevant at this load, and the rewrite gives up the property that both counts change at once

options.text: Keep the synchronized version, since 2 AtomicLongs updated from 16 threads lose some of their increments
options.says: each AtomicLong loses nothing; the defect is a reader seeing one count changed and the other not

options.text: Switch to the rewrite, since 7 million a second is about 175 times the 40,000 peak it has to carry
options.says: both are far above the peak, so the extra headroom buys nothing, and the rewrite brings back the torn read

options.text: Switch to the rewrite, since 2 AtomicLongs updated from 16 threads keep both counts as exact as 1 lock
options.says: each count is exact on its own, but a reader can see one changed and the other not, which one lock prevents

origin.section: Simplicity Costs Throughput Under Contention: Measure It Against the Load You Have

concepts: The simple design can be slower under heavy contention, and the decision weighs measured capacity against the stated load.
Every point where another thread can run between two steps of a shared operation multiplies the schedules: one step per method gives 3! orders for three calls, split steps give many more.
A stress test runs the schedules timing makes likely, so it seldom meets a race that an exhaustive model finds in a large share of schedules.
